  - A rescue that failed blanked `via` until the next answer, and a turn interrupted mid-rescue kept saying `slow · trying X…` for up to ten minutes. The rescue now has a slot beside the last sighting, so a failed one hands the row back to the machine that answered last. A rescue is only promised while the turn runs.
  - A title or memory errand finishing on another lane overwrote the answer's sighting and blanked `via`. Hidden roles no longer reach the status line's desk.
  - `via` appeared only once a whole step had finished, so the first answer, or a follow-up after ten quiet minutes, showed none while it was being written. It now names the machine the live phase reports.
  - The conversation's rate and machine were filed under its model id, which moves between the engine and the window (a mid-turn pick, a fallback hop, a change from another window). They are now filed under the conversation first. The `phase` and `lane` wire frames carry `session`, and an older host without it still reads by model.
  - An engine host from before the news frames sent no provider or rate, and nothing said so. The welcome now carries `news`. A window whose engine sends neither the flag nor any news frame says once, after an answer, that its engine is an older aforge.

  The wire version does not change. A status line must not refuse a conversation, so the older-engine case is reported with a note and never refused.

  </details>

- **a keystroke is not refused at ten seconds behind an unrelated getter** — [#846](https://github.com/Agent-Field/codeaf/pull/846) · `chat` `remote`

  <details><summary>5 things that are no longer true</summary>

  - The engine's read loop dispatched every call serially. A getter held the reader and a keystroke behind it waited out `callDeadline` (10s), then the surface was told `the connection to the engine is gone` while the engine went on to apply the answer. Getters and small acts now run off the reader; stream-opening and shape-changing calls stay on it, in order. `classify` in `internal/remote/callclass.go` is the one predicate.
  - A timeout answered with `Client.gone` — `the connection to <machine> is gone` — about a link that was carrying that turn's events at that moment. It never buried anything (only the reader calls `Client.bury`, on a pipe that actually failed); the sentence was the whole of the damage, and the surface believed it. A timeout on a live connection now says `<machine> did not answer in time`, and `Client.gone` is kept for a pipe that broke.
  - A LONGER DEADLINE FOR A PERSON'S ACT IS THE FIX THAT DOES NOT WORK, and it was tried on this branch before it was taken out — anyone reaching for it again should read `callclass.go` first. `answerQuestion` asks its door straight from the update loop, so a 30s act window is 30s a terminal can sit without drawing: eighteen copies of the questions e2e six at a time gave two 53-second copies against 22 for every other, both losing the receipt, where twelve copies of the parent gave none over 33. `callDeadline` stays one window for every call; the road is what stops an act needing more.
  - `app.answerQuestion` swallowed `ResolveQuestion`'s error (`if err != nil { return nil }`). A refused act is now said on screen in the door's own words, through `app.note`, the same door rewind, autonomy, connect and a permission already use.
  - The questions manual said a window over `--host` cannot yet answer. It can: the key crosses to the engine that owns the work, and a refusal comes back in that engine's own words.

  Measured on 2026-09-10: six copies of `TestQuestionsE2E/TheOrdinaryRoadCarriesAQuestionAndItsAnswer`
  at once, and one of them spent exactly ten seconds — `internal/remote`'s
  `callDeadline` — before the surface logged `REFUSED err=the connection to the
  engine is gone`, while the engine had applied the answer and the model had
  already said `They picked "delete it"`. The five that passed round-tripped in
  one millisecond. The receipt half of that (a key drawn as `another window`)
  landed on the diet branch; this is the road.

  </details>

- **a later task is not pointed at an earlier task's copy** — [#847](https://github.com/Agent-Field/codeaf/pull/847) · `engine` `chat`

  <details><summary>3 things that are no longer true</summary>

  - `taskCopy.bind` moved two folders — the node's ground (#566) and the conversation's own `work/` (#804) — so a contract that named an EARLIER TREE of the same conversation (`<session>/trees/1/…`) was left exactly as written, and the worker standing in `<session>/trees/2` was refused `is outside your copy` about a directory the harness itself had invented. `taskCopyFor` now reads `Place.Trees()` from the same record the copy was cut from and binds another tree of this conversation to the same path under this copy. The ground rule still wins where both could apply, an address already inside this worker's own copy stands as written, and a path that is genuinely somewhere else on the machine is untouched and still earns the refusal — `taskoutside.go` is unchanged, and #566's guard is not widened. The person's own quoted words are still never rewritten.
  - A contract whose only address was under another tree of this conversation named no file under the ground as far as `groundNamesWorkUnder` could see, so `groundMode` made the work a REFERENCE — a folder that is deliberately not a copy of its ground, and therefore binds nothing. Naming a file in another tree of this conversation is now naming work under the ground, so such a task is given a branch of the person's repository like any other. The node's provenance does not move: its ground stays the person's repository and its copy stays `trees/<its own id>`.
  - `internal/manual/chat/how-tasks-run.md` said a path that is not under the project is left exactly as written, with the conversation's own `work` folder as the one exception. Another task's copy under this conversation's `trees/` is an exception too, and the page states it with the before-and-after address under the heading "A later task is not pointed at an earlier task's copy".

  Issue #839, found by the whole tagged e2e package — where it fired once in five
  runs of `TestAWorktreeTaskFollowsItsContractInsideItsOwnCopy` while the subtest
  alone always passed — and then pinned deterministically by
  `TestASecondTaskIsNotPointedAtTheFirstTasksCopy`, which cuts two trees for one
  conversation in the order the package cuts them. The conversation learns the
  address of a task's private copy honestly, from the first worker's own report,
  so the model that proposes the next piece of work writes that address into WHAT
  TO PRODUCE; what was wrong was the handoff, not the model and not the guard.

  </details>

- **a retry goes to a different machine, and the ledger is keyed on who answered** — [#850](https://github.com/Agent-Field/codeaf/pull/850) · `chat` `engine` `docs`

  <details><summary>12 things that are no longer true</summary>

  - A retry re-sent the bytes encoded once above `provider/retry.go`'s attempt loop, so `provider.order` / `only` / `ignore` were fixed for the whole call and every attempt went to the same machine — 53 % of ten days of multi-attempt chains never left the lane they started on, and three spent sixteen and seventeen consecutive sends on one machine over eleven minutes. The body is now written per attempt, with the machines that refused THIS CALL dropped from it (`refusedHere` → `callKnobs.refused` → `wirePreferences`'s `dropRefusedHere`). `velocity.go`'s own sentence, 'the retries of the call that drew the 429 still wait it out, because their body is already written', is deleted.
  - The exclusion keys on the machine that ANSWERED, never on the machine we asked for. `provider.order` is advisory once `allow_fallbacks` is true: in the 2026-09-10 22:20 run every attempt asked for DeepInfra and Parasail answered eighteen 429s on one node, so re-ordering excluded nothing. The next body carries `provider.ignore: [the `(via X)` in the refusal]`, and the lane we asked for is left in the order and never struck — it did not answer, so it has said nothing.
  - `retryElsewhere` and `demandedPoolIsFull` (#835) were two exits answering one question and could disagree — a 429 naming a rescue's machine went back to the race, a 502 naming it did not. They are one door now, `Client.handBack`: a strict pin never hands back, a refused demand goes back at once, an account-wide pacing never does, and everything else goes back when the race can fund an alternative.
  - `Retry-After` was read from the header only, and the census recorded it on not one row in ten days while every fourth failure was a 429 — this router names its comeback in the refusal envelope. `retryAfterIn` now reads `retry_after` beside the error, on it, and in its metadata, still capped at `maxProviderWait`.
  - A 429 that named no pool was always an account-wide limit and wrote nothing. Under a demand of exactly one machine it is now filed against that machine, because a demand of one machine IS the whole serving set. With nothing demanded it still writes nothing.
  - `velocity.go`'s refusal door and its two paces were switched off by configuration — `c.velocity == nil || !c.carriesPreferences() || routing == RoutingOff` — so with routing off, or on a base that had not yet shown it carries a preference, nothing was paced, struck or learned while every other controller went on acting. The ledger always records now; only what is EMITTED from it is configured, which was already gated at `providerPreferences` and `laneChoiceFor`. A base that is not a router gets a ledger with one row, not no ledger. `TestRoutingOffSendsNoPreferencesAndMeasuresNothing`, `TestRoutingOffTeachesTheBeliefNothing` and `TestRoutingOffNotesNothingForACut` are renamed and inverted; the manual's 'Only `off` stops both' is replaced.
  - A `Tools:false` lane was never tried. `internal/lane/frontier.go` removed it from every tool-carrying request for good on a router flag this build had already measured wrong — the 2026-09-10 screenshot has GMICloud gated out of a request while it was serving that same task's tool calls six seconds at a time. `Tools`, `Uptime5m` and `Status` are priors now: a doubted lane is ranked behind every lane nothing is doubted about (`sheetDoubtsLast`), one request in ten probes it first, and a lane whose own answers have come back usable is not doubted at all — a belief that decays back toward the sheet's prior on `QualityHalfLife`. `frontier.go`'s `toolsLast` is `sheetDoubtsLast`. `Serves`, the wire's own negative, stays the one hard exclusion.
  - A stream cut that named no server struck nothing, so `StreamCut.Rerouted` was false and the next attempt went back to the same lane deterministically — the one stall shape that could not reroute. It is now filed against the machine this request asked for (`provider.only` of one, else `provider.order[0]`, else a rescue's demand), which this process wrote itself. `Rerouted` is false only for a request that expressed no preference at all.
  - A 429 was answered by waiting. The owner's ruling of 2026-09-10 — 'we need to handle not yet properly', nobody works a rate limit around by switching models themselves — is now the contract in code: the machine that said it comes off the next body and the next body goes out AT ONCE, with no backoff, because a backoff is what we pay to ask the SAME machine again. When every machine this request may use is held at once, a watched call hands the refusal straight back so `pacingExhausted` offers the next model (endpoints.go), and only a call nobody is watching waits — for the window the machine itself named, with that moment on `notePhase(PhasePaced…)` so a surface draws a real countdown instead of our doubling.
  - `WithPatientRateLimits` meant 'sixty attempts against one machine'. It means 'may wait for the earliest window when there is nowhere else to go'; a patient call walks the machines exactly as a watched one does and reaches a wait by the same road. `patience.go`'s header says so.
  - `provider.order` was treated as a way to steer a retry. It is a RANKING the router may ignore once `allow_fallbacks` is true; only `provider.ignore` takes a machine off the table, and that is what the next body now carries.
  - `Client.refuseUpstream` returned a bool. It returns the `laneRefusal` it acted on, so the retry loop can read which machine must be off the next body without classifying the same refusal a second time.

  Two new structural laws ride the `laws` gate: `TestNoLedgerWriteIsKeyedOnTheLaneWeChose` (`internal/provider/servedkey_law_test.go`) fails the build the day a ledger write takes a lane we merely chose — 3,728 of 10,107 finished attempts came back from a machine that was not the one chosen, and `lane: Fireworks` / `via DeepInfra` appears 104 times, so the wrong argument is both common and compiles. `TestRetryNeverRepeatsAMachine` runs 200 randomised scripted pools and fails on any identical (machine, body) pair sent twice while another machine was admissible.

  Replicated end to end before the fix, in `internal/provider/neverrepeat_test.go`: a three-machine pool with two saturated answered in six sends to one machine and then failed; it answers in three now, one to each machine, with `2 of 6` on the status row and no status code anywhere a person can read. The tool-carrying screenshot (`TestATaskIsAnsweredByTheLaneTheSheetDoubts`) is answered by the machine the sheet flags `Tools:false`.

  </details>

- **a window that just acted is still watching, and a stop names the door it really came through** — [#851](https://github.com/Agent-Field/codeaf/pull/851) · `chat` `engine` `remote`

  <details><summary>3 things that are no longer true</summary>

  - Every road that ended a hosted conversation cancelled the turn as `session retired` and read out the unattended door's sentence, `nobody was left watching this conversation, so the reply stopped`. That is now the unattended door's alone: a person's own goodbye is `conversation left`, a host stopped on somebody's word while a window is still in the room is a new door, `engine stopped`, and only the sweep and a torn one-shot pipe still say nobody was watching.
  - A hosted conversation with no surface attached was unwatched on the instant, so a call that stalled past internal/remote's ten-second callDeadline tore the pipe and emptied a room the person was sitting in. A window that made a call inside `watchGrace` — twice that deadline, the stalled call and the redial after it — now counts as somebody watching, in the sweep (remote.Session.RetireIfIdle) and in the stand-down reading (enginehost.Host.idleLocked) alike.
  - A stop the unattended door takes used to say only that nobody was left watching. It now names the window it believed had gone when it has one to name — `nobody was left watching this conversation from studio, so the reply stopped — ask again to pick it up` — because the cause carries the label (session.Agent.InterruptNamed).

  #833 is a reply that stopped with `bash · cancelled` and the unattended sentence
  while its window was on the screen and the person had just pressed a key on a
  card in it. The surface's call had refused at the ten-second deadline (#832) and
  the torn pipe made the room look empty. Presence is renewed by the act itself
  now, and a stop taken anyway says which door it came through.

  </details>

- **One classifier for every failed call — the transport states facts, one function picks the move** — [#854](https://github.com/Agent-Field/codeaf/pull/854) · `engine` `chat`

  <details><summary>12 things that are no longer true</summary>

  - A 404 was classified by three unrelated rules — internal/taxonomy's `classOf`, internal/provider's `refusalKind`, internal/session's `providerCouldNotServe` — each correct about the half it had been told and each growing a special case every wave. There is now one: the transport decides STRUCTURAL FACTS once at its refusal door and carries them typed (`APIError.Routing`, `.Account`, `.Withdrawn`, `.Overflow`, `.Code`), `provider.Evidence(err)` is the one extractor and makes no decision, and `taxonomy.Classify` is the only function in the tree that turns evidence into a class and an action. A law test (`internal/taxonomy/classifier_law_test.go`) fails the build on a `.Status` compared against 400 or above outside internal/taxonomy and internal/provider.
  - internal/session's turn loop ran `isContextOverflow(errMsg) || !isRetryable(errMsg)` over the provider's prose and RETURNED on it, forty lines after the verdict had read the same failure off typed evidence — a string deciding what a typed classification had already answered. `isContextOverflow` and its seven-branch regex are deleted; `isRetryable` remains as EVIDENCE for `taxonomy.Evidence.Wire` and decides nothing. A context overflow is structural now: the request-too-large status and the error envelope's own `code`, with the sentence kept only as a last-resort hint inside the transport.
  - `taxonomy` had three classes. It has four: `Shape` is the REQUEST — a transcript longer than the window, or bytes the router itself read and refused — and its moves are real, `ActionCompact` (once per turn) and `ActionReshape`. A 4xx that named no upstream used to be `Work`, the same word a job that could not be done gets, so a turn ended blaming somebody's request for their conversation.
  - A spent relaxation ladder (`provider.RefusalError`) was read as `taxonomy.Work` and ended the turn with the router's own sentence on screen while a chain the person had configured sat unasked. It is `Evidence.Spent` now: `Transport` with its budget declared gone, whose one move is the caller's chain. `provider.RoutingRefusal` still answers false for one — there is no machine and no shape left THERE — and that is a different question from "was anything learned".
  - `Verdict` named two exported types in packages that call each other: internal/taxonomy's control answer and internal/provider's learning record. The learning record is `provider.Reading` (file `reading.go`, constants `Reading*`), internal/lane's watch answer is `lane.Advice`, and `TestOnlyOneVerdictTypeExists` holds the module to one. Struct FIELDS named `Verdict` that carry a `provider.Reading` keep their names and their JSON tags, because those are on disk in profile records and plan graphs.
  - The refusal door asked `canWalk()` — a PREDICTION that the walk would carry a refusal — and then `deferLadder(body)` to record that it had relied on one; #835 added `exhausted()` to catch the misses, so the prediction and its repair both existed. There is one call now, `takeRefusal(body)`, which asks and records in the same critical section, so the answer and the promise cannot disagree. `exhausted()` is the fulfilment of that promise rather than a repair. `canWalk` survives only as `walkAvailable`, a reading with one caller (retry.go's `retryElsewhere`) that is not a handoff.
  - TWO mechanisms changed a request's model from one `FallbackModels` list: `endpoints.go`'s `fallbackChain` walk at the foot of the relaxation ladder, `recoverFromPacing`, and internal/session's turn loop — none of them knowing the others had already tried a model. Both adapter walks are deleted; the relaxation rungs stay, the adapter never changes the model, and `session`'s `ActionHop` is the only model change in the build. Live evidence from 2026-09-10 22:32 says why coordinating them was not enough: the adapter's hop carried the ORIGINAL model's `provider.only` across to the new model and was answered `404 No allowed providers are available for the selected model`, because a lane pin is per model and nothing re-derived it. The person-facing `Retry 1/1: Falling back to <model>` line is gone with it; the turn's own `moving to <model>` line is what a person reads.
  - `nextFallback` picked the next model by indexing the chain with a count it kept itself — `options[len(hopped)]` — which is only right while nothing else hops. It reads `provider.ModelsTried(ctx)`, a per-turn record every send writes at the one door it passes through, and answers with the first model on the chain that is on neither list.
  - A model the router carries with ZERO endpoints was indistinguishable from an emptied endpoint set: the same 404, the same sentence, and it spent the whole transport budget buying three more identical refusals before the hop that was the only move all along (measured 2026-09-10 22:39 — three sends thirty milliseconds apart, every turn, and the next turn hopped somewhere else because nothing remembered). It is `Evidence.Withdrawn` now, decided structurally (`Client.withdrawnModel`), hops at once with no budget spent, and is remembered by the adapter that learned it — one client, which is one conversation: a later turn's request is not sent at all and the chain does not offer the model. An answer clears the memory; nothing is written to disk.
  - The empty-200 re-ask took the boundary's verdict, took the wait, and told the surface NOTHING — no `EventRetrying`, no `RetryNews`, no phase — so a person watched a clock counting a request that had already come back empty. It now emits one `EventRetrying` (`nothing came back from the model — asking again`) with its `RetryNews`, and narrates a non-zero wait on the same phase pipe the ladder uses.
  - A turn that ended on a provider failure handed out the router's own sentence — `API error (404): 0 endpoints out of 1 requested are available matching your guardrail restrictions and data policy`. It never does: `endingWords` puts the boundary's person-facing sentence in front, with the typed failure reachable underneath so every layer that decides by type still can. The new sentences are `that model is not being served any more`, `your key was not accepted for this model`, `this conversation got too long for the model`, `this conversation is too long for the model even after shortening it` and `the request could not be sent as it was`, and `internal/manual/chat/models-and-cost.md` has the table.
  - `provider.RefusalError.Tried` named the fallback models the adapter had walked. The adapter walks none, so the field is deleted and its advice branch with it; the layer that hops says what it tried, in its own words, because it is the layer that knows.

  This is `docs/design/recovery/DESIGN.md` §7 row R2, and the defect it closes is not
  a wrong line anywhere. Four waves in two weeks each added a correct special case to
  a DIFFERENT rule about what a failed call meant, and #835 had to add
  `Evidence.Routing` to work around one of them. The shape that allows that is what
  this removes: the transport states facts, one function turns facts into a move, and
  three go/ast laws fail the build on the next site that tries to answer for itself.

  </details>

- **a correction that fell through gets its turn drawn — the steer lane is stamped by conversation** — [#855](https://github.com/Agent-Field/codeaf/pull/855) · `chat`

  <details><summary>2 things that are no longer true</summary>

  - A turn the engine answered was believed to always reach the screen. It was not: a correction typed into a running answer that fell through — the turn ended before a boundary came — carried its own stream across the seam, and the surface's lane was stamped with app.gen, the TURN generation. app.gen moves on every submit, every adopted stream and every drained follow-up, so the stamp was stale by the time a fall-through was read (which is, by definition, after a turn ended). app.steerFell drained that channel and threw it away: the engine ran the turn, paid for it and journaled the answer, and the window drew neither the question nor a word of the reply. The lane now carries app.steerGen, which moves only when the conversation on screen is replaced (detach.go).
  - A conversation that had answered a question and shown nothing was read as the model having gone silent. It was the surface: reopening the same conversation shows the answers the live window never drew, because the journal had them all along. A blank turn is now a bug report about tui3, not about the model or the router.

  Measured on 2026-09-10 22:39: three `whats up` messages in a row, three answers
  in `transcript.jsonl`, and a screen that showed none of them. Plain enter over a
  running answer steers (input.go), the answer ended before a boundary came, and
  each correction became a turn of its own on a stream the surface then discarded
  for having the wrong turn number on it.

  Beside the fix, two pins on the other road into the same law — a turn that hopped
  to a fallback model draws the answer that model wrote, and the calls it made
  after the hop keep their rows.

  </details>

- **A hosted conversation keeps drawing the turns the engine starts after this window's own first turn** — [#856](https://github.com/Agent-Field/codeaf/pull/856) · `chat`

  <details><summary>5 things that are no longer true</summary>

  - It was believed that a wake — the turn the engine starts when a task lands — always reached the attached window (wakelane.go's fix). It did not once the window had run a turn of its own: watchFollowing carried the TURN generation (app.gen), every typed turn bumps it, so the next Following was discarded as a turn from a connection the window had left and the wait was never re-armed. Every wake after that went to the journal only. The waits now carry app.linkGen, which only a conversation switch bumps.
  - The keyboard lane (watchDriving / drivingMoved) had the same shape and the same fix; a hand-over after this window's own turn is heard and the wait re-armed.
  - #855 gave the steer lane its own conversation generation (app.steerGen) for the same defect one lane over. There is now ONE such counter for the three lanes, app.convGen, bumped where a switch replaces the conversation; steerGen and linkGen do not exist.
  - PR #699 (2026-09-09) was the same fix for the two connection lanes and sat unmerged until it conflicted with dev; its manual paragraph on how-tasks-run.md rides here and the PR is closed as superseded.
  - This was invisible in the in-process launch, which draws wakes through the local wake lane, and in a scratch home whose path is over the 104-byte unix-socket limit, because such a launch silently falls back to in-process. Reproduce it on a daemon: a short AFORGE_HOME, a quick task that lands, one typed turn first.

  Seen 2026-09-10 in a conversation on the workspace daemon: three quick tasks
  landed, the engine wrote its sentences about them, `whats up` was answered twice
  in the journal, and the screen showed a task card and empty turns until the
  conversation was reopened.

  </details>

- **the router can reach the fast lanes again, and a refusal now counts against a lane** — [#859](https://github.com/Agent-Field/codeaf/pull/859) · `engine` `chat`

  <details><summary>4 things that are no longer true</summary>

  - A request the belief had ordered carried `max_price` = list × 1.25, which vetoed every lane more than a quarter dearer than the cheapest before the order was read. The ceiling is now raised until every lane the order names fits under it; a named lane whose tariff is unknown raises it by nothing.
  - A task node was routed at λ = 0 — price only, frontier pruned to 1.25× the cheapest. λ now has a floor of a quarter of a person's attention (`lane.UnattendedValue`); only the routing row's `price` word means zero.
  - A 429 or a struck lane reached the strike ledger and never the belief. It is now an `Outcome{Refused: true}` on a new availability axis (`Belief.Availability`, five-minute half-life) that divides the expected wait; quality is not charged for it.
  - No lane was ever too slow in absolute terms. A service floor — 6 s first token, 15 tok/s, half of requests answered, on a belief the ledger is sure about — refuses it, and never empties the set.

  Three days of the call log put the router's mean regret on deepseek-v4.1-flash at
  31.9 s against 1.2 s with these changes replayed
  (`docs/design/routing/ASSESSMENT-20260911.md`; `go test -tags replay ./internal/lane/`
  is the bench). Censored timing for cut streams is still owed.

  </details>

- **a decayed belief draws no tail, and the greeting's spend test stops turning on the hour** — [#862](https://github.com/Agent-Field/codeaf/pull/862) · `chat`

  <details><summary>3 things that are no longer true</summary>

  - The lane picker decided a belief had aged past saying anything about its worst case by catching the OVERFLOW: a lane nobody had heard from since yesterday had a p99 of +Inf, and `laneTail`'s IsInf arm refused it. #852's `lane.MaxSpread` clamp — a floor under the arithmetic, not a judgement — made that p99 finite, so the same belief arrived at the ceiling (σ ≈ 2.4, p99 ≈ 212 s against an 800 ms median) and the row drew `tail 212.7s`. Vagueness is now read off the BELIEF (`laneTailOf`: a spread at `lane.MaxSpread` draws nothing at all — not a figure, and not `no tail`, which is a claim about the worst case too). `laneTail`'s own arithmetic gate is unchanged.
  - `TestTheGreetingsFirstFrameCarriesTheSpend` was believed to be a regression #857 or #849 introduced. It is neither: it wrote its ledger line an hour before a real `time.Now()`, and `today` is a calendar day in the person's own zone (`session.SpendToday`) — so it was green for twenty-three hours a day and red for the hour after midnight, at #842 where it landed and at every commit since. The surface's arithmetic was right on both sides of midnight and does not move; `homeLab` grew a pinned clock (`homeLab.pin`, midday of the day it is asked for) and the test writes its fixture against that.
  - A `homeLab` test whose subject is a calendar day — a `today`, a fortnight, a `yesterday` — must call `homeLab.pin` before `homeLab.app` rather than passing `time.Now()` around. A lab that pins nothing still reads the real wall clock, which is right for every test whose subject is not a date.

  Both were on `dev` with nothing in `.github/known-red.txt` naming them, and
  neither goes on it: that ledger only shrinks. Proved by `internal/tui3` in full
  on the Spark with `-count=1`, and the two named tests run across a sweep of
  zones that put the wall clock at 23:52, 00:52 and 04:52.

  </details>

- **the parity bench's own verdict, corrected — one regression, one flake, and a grep read as a screen** — [#866](https://github.com/Agent-Field/codeaf/pull/866) · `docs`

  <details><summary>4 things that are no longer true</summary>

  - docs/design/prompt-diet/BENCH.md §1a landed saying TWO subtests regressed on the prompt diet. One did. `TestTUIE2E/space_in_the_task_room_pages_the_card` was FLAKE: it failed once at 249s against the baseline's 71.7s because the task landed `your call · ran 2m 8s` where the baseline's landed `done · ran 10s`, so two 30-second waits blew before the paging assertion was reached — and on two further runs a side it passed 2/2 on both. The draft was written before those repeats came back and says so in a sentence ("Both are candidates, not verdicts") that is easy to read past. Anyone acting on it would have spent a day hunting a behaviour change that never happened.
  - The same section said the failing screen of `TestQuestionsE2E/TheOrdinaryRoadCarriesAQuestionAndItsAnswer` "contains `· you ·` elsewhere in the same dump" and might therefore be a frame race. It does not. That match was the TEST'S OWN ERROR TEXT — `the screen never said " · you · "` — counted as though it were screen content, because a grep count was read instead of the lines it matched. The screen carries `· another window ·` twice and `· you ·` nowhere, which makes the finding stronger rather than weaker: there is no race, the word was simply wrong.
  - That subtest WAS a real regression on `prompt-diet/integrate` at 2a90be7e8 — 3/3 fail there against 3/3 pass on the `dev` baseline at 6aa6a946e, the same assertion and the same wrong word every time, on the attribution of an answer the person gave in their own window. It is NOT on the trunk: the same subtest against `dev` at c9f24f2b6, after the wave merged as #844, passes 3/3. Whatever spelled that row `· another window ·` was fixed before the merge landed, so the finding is a record of what the bench caught and where, and there is nothing to fix in the code.
  - Both errors in the landed draft came from reading a grep count instead of the lines it matched — the same shape as the 94%-cut figure BENCH.md §1b already records one layer up, where a median over every request measured the mix of call kinds rather than the size of the prompt. §1a now carries its own account of what it got wrong, beside §1b, because a bench whose corrections live only in a changelog is a bench whose next reader repeats them.

  The prompt-diet wave's evidence page was written while its own confirmation runs
  were still in flight, and merged with the draft's wording. The repeats landed
  afterwards and said something different from what the page claims.

  The rule this breaks is #176's, and the bench states it: reproduce a red on a
  live-model suite before calling it a regression, do not rerun it in isolation and
  move on. The repeats were queued and the page was written anyway. What this
  change lands is the answer they gave.

  </details>

- **Opening a task's page or switching tabs no longer counts the token figures up from zero** — [#867](https://github.com/Agent-Field/codeaf/pull/867) · `chat` `docs`

  <details><summary>1 thing that is no longer true</summary>

  - Every page opened its token column at nothing and walked the first reading up from zero with the glow lit, so opening a task from the rail or taking a conversation up from a tab replayed the climb to the same figures on every visit. A figure coming onto the screen is now drawn whole and unlit on the first frame (tokencol.go's chaseFigure); only a rise after it walks and glows. A climbing, lit figure now always means something actually arrived.

  The owner switched between two running tasks and watched `↑ 79.6k  ↓ 37.6k`
  count up and light up each time, and read a page being built as a task being
  busy. The `+3.4k` receipt already treated a first reading as a figure arriving
  rather than growing; the walk and the glow now keep the same rule.

  </details>

- **A conversation that ran a quick task reopens with its task graph** — [#869](https://github.com/Agent-Field/codeaf/pull/869) · `engine` `chat`

  <details><summary>3 things that are no longer true</summary>

  - A quick task's empty acceptance was harmless. It was not: the checkpoint's validator refused any node with no acceptance, and its refusal is whole-document, so ONE quick task anywhere in a conversation's history threw the WHOLE task graph away on the way back in — every finished row, every piece of running work, the whole family — leaving one line in a log file saying the checkpoint was corrupt. Now whether a node owes an acceptance is a property of its KIND, declared once in `kindsWithoutAcceptance` and read through `acceptanceHolds`; a quick node's blank is the answer, and everything else is refused exactly as strictly as before.
  - A quick node that was WAITING ITS TURN when the window closed used to be unreachable (the whole file was refused). Now the file loads, and that node SETTLES rather than going back on the frontier: its list is not in the checkpoint, and `runTaskNode` dispatches on that list, so a resumed one would have been handed to an ordinary worker with a copy of the folder, a branch and a check. Its row reads `the quick task never started before aforge closed, and it does not resume — ask for it again`. A quick node that was RUNNING settles as it always did.
  - The manual said nothing about what a quick task leaves behind a restart. `internal/manual/chat/tasks.md` now has *A quick task after a restart*, per state, and `how-tasks-run.md`'s row 5b names the quick exception beside the design's.

  Found on a real checkpoint: four `quick` nodes with `"acceptance": ""` beside three
  ordinary ones, and a conversation that reopened with nothing in its column. The fix is
  not a placeholder "DONE WHEN" for quick nodes — nothing would ever read one — but a
  single declaration of which kinds carry an acceptance, read by the builder that leaves
  the field empty and by the validator that refuses a record without one, with a law test
  over the builders so the two cannot drift apart again.

  The record's own shape — carrying a quick node's line, items, ticks and files so a
  queued one can resume as a quick node rather than settling — is a separate change.

  </details>

- **a question you talk past comes down, and your own words go out at once** — [#870](https://github.com/Agent-Field/codeaf/pull/870) · `chat` `engine` `docs`

  <details><summary>9 things that are no longer true</summary>

  - An interrupted turn could sit idle for a minute before resuming. What was actually happening was worse and had no clock in it at all: a sentence typed while an `ask` question stood open queued behind that question, and the question was waiting for the same sentence, so NO REQUEST WAS EVER MADE. Measured 2026-09-10 in two conversations — seven minutes and fifty-two seconds in one, until the person pressed Escape, which then dropped their words with the stopped turn. A steer now ends every `ask` this session is parked on, and the next request is on the wire inside `lane.SpokenWithin`.
  - A parked `ask` had two endings — answered, or its own lane let go — held in a bare `Agent.askWaits` map that four files reached into with their own delete-then-touch. It has THREE, and they are named methods on one type with the rule in its doc comment (`internal/session/askwait.go`): `answerLocked`, `talkedPastLocked`, `letGoLocked`. The map is gone; nothing outside that file may touch the channels.
  - Two maps hold one question — the wait (`askwait.go`) and the words every surface draws (`Agent.questionWords`) — and only the first was claimed under the lock. Closing the channel makes the `ask` lane runnable at once, and the first thing it does is its own deferred withdrawal with `questionGoneReason`'s `the turn moved on without it`, so which sentence the person read about their own act was a race. Both are claimed in one locked section now (`claimQuestionLocked`), and `WithdrawQuestion` is the claim plus `sayWithdrawn` rather than a body of its own.
  - `internal/manual/chat/screen.md` and `keys.md` listed four steer landings and said the clause `is one of` them. There is a fifth, `took this instead of the question`, and it is in both lists.
  - `internal/manual/chat/questions.md` said an ask-back (`?`) sends the question and `its reply lands in the conversation` with the block still there to answer. While the work is PARKED ON THAT QUESTION it does not: the sentence rides the ordinary steering queue and reaches the model only once the question is answered. The page says so now, in the `?` section and in the two places that repeat the promise. The underlying wedge is the questions lane's to rule on, not this change's.
  - `internal/manual/chat/questions.md` said that with nothing pressed, what you type is a message to the conversation and THE QUESTION WAITS. It does not wait: sending a message takes the question back, the row reads `no longer needed · you said something else instead`, and your own line is marked `took this instead of the question`.
  - A question released this way is not an answer and is recorded as none: the `ask` tool hands the model a sentence saying nobody answered and that the person's words are the next thing it will read, and no `DecisionRecord` is written. A model that assumed a released question had been answered with a default is wrong.
  - A call the caller abandoned had its end row in the log by the time the call returned, and `TestAnAbandonedStreamStillEndsItsRow` and `TestEveryStartRowGetsARowUnderIt` both asserted it synchronously. The row is an EVENTUAL fact now — still written, still collected within `abandonGrace`, still impossible to lose — but no longer on the caller's way out. A reader of the log at the instant a cancelled call returns may see a start row whose end row is a few milliseconds behind it — which the census reads as a call still in flight, so a reader of the log takes its tally once the arms have reported. Every other clause of the honesty law (opened once, ended once, never ended without going out) is unchanged.
  - `hedgeRace.abandon` — reached exactly when a person's steer cancelled the race — drained its arms for up to `abandonGrace` BEFORE answering its caller, so a cancelled call could spend the whole of `lane.SpokenWithin` in front of somebody who had just typed a correction. The drain and the two budget notes are `hedgeRace.accountForTheAbandoned` now, on a guarded goroutine nobody waits on; the caller gets `ctx.Err()` immediately. ONLY A WAIT went behind the caller — the offer still comes down inside `abandon`, because withdrawing it posts a phase, and a phase posted from behind that return would land after the call's own closing one, under the subject the next request has since filed its own phase under, blanking it. `spokenWaitExceptions`'s reason for `(*hedgeRace).drainArms` changed with it — it is not in the request path any more, rather than being in it with nobody listening.

  There is no resume branch and no new timer: the turn goes back round
  `Agent.runTurn`'s own loop, through the same drain and the same send every other
  step uses, carrying the question's result and then the person's words. What was
  missing was an ending for the wait, not a road back from it.

  </details>

- **Nothing auxiliary blocks the person — one reading beside the work, never in front of it** — [#871](https://github.com/Agent-Field/codeaf/pull/871) · `chat` `engine`

  <details><summary>20 things that are no longer true</summary>

  - THE MAIN CALL NO LONGER WAITS FOR THE PRE-TURN RECALL. `Agent.refreshMemory` was a line of `Agent.runTurn` (loop.go:318), awaited, so the person's own model was not asked anything until a reflex machine had answered — the call census of 2026-09-11 measured sixteen of them at a mean of 4.3s and a maximum of 10.7s, on every single message. It is started in `Agent.startTurnLocked` beside the title now (`Agent.startRecallLocked`, memory.go) and read at the wire. `refreshMemory` returns a bool — whether the block MOVED — where it returned nothing.
  - A MARK READING NO LONGER PAUSES THE WORK. `Agent.readMark` was awaited at loop.go's step boundary through `Agent.checkpointRound`, and a measured one held a turn for 8.1 seconds between a tool result and the next step to decide nothing (`checkpointSketch.split` is false on nearly every reading). It is started at the boundary that crosses the mark and SPENT at the next one (`Agent.checkpointSettle`, new, called at the head of the loop exactly the way `Agent.routeTriage` spends the work-or-words race). `Agent.checkpointRound` takes a `*markAside` argument, and so does `Agent.checkpointReopen`. The CEILING's own reading stays awaited, because by then the turn is already being moved and there is no next step to run beside — and so is a drawing crossed by the round that ENDS a turn (`Agent.closeMarkAside`, new): it has no next boundary either, and a mastermind call paid for and thrown away is a ledger line nobody can ever count.
  - `preparing saved context` IS GONE FROM THE SCREEN. It was an honest sentence about a wait that no longer exists, and a phase word for a reading nobody is behind would be the status line naming its own machinery. `internal/tui3/phase_test.go` still POSTS that phase as fixture data and still renders it correctly; nothing in internal/session posts it any more. The manual page that explained it (`what-i-remember.md`) now explains why it went.
  - `sidecar.settle` IS `sidecar.takeAtTheEnd`, AND THE NAME IS THE LAW. The blocking read is spelled for the only condition under which it is honest, so `sidecar_law_test.go` can hold every caller of it to the same ending-road property it holds an awaited reading to — `readBeside(ctx, …).settle()` inside `runTurn` satisfied every clause of the old law and restored the whole 4.3-second gate. `Agent.closeMarkAside` is gone; its work is four lines of `runTurn`'s own exit defer, where the tree can see that the turn has ended. And the law's watched set is now DERIVED — whatever a `readBeside` ask calls is a reading, so one added tomorrow under a name nobody has thought of is on the law the day it lands — and an ending door exempts the run of statements that reaches it rather than the whole function it appears in. Three planted shapes that each passed the old law are in the file, asserted to be named by the new one.
  - `act` RUNS BEFORE THE ANSWER CAN BE TAKEN, AND A READING THAT WAS LET GO OF INTERRUPTS NOTHING (sidecar.go). The settle used to close first, so a taker could spend an answer against a step the interruption was still about to cut; and `end` did not stop `act`, so a mark's cut could land on the NEXT turn's generation. Both are ordering, both are one line.
  - THE THREE AD-HOC SIDECAR GOROUTINES ARE ONE MECHANISM. `internal/session/sidecar.go` declares `sidecar[T]` and `readBeside(ctx, ask, act)` — start where the question becomes askable, `take` where the answer can still be spent (non-blocking), `end` where nobody can spend it, `settle` only where there is genuinely nothing left to run beside. `routeRace` no longer holds its own `stop`/`settled`/`spent`; `routeRace.yes` is `sidecar.take`. Anyone adding a reading beside a turn uses this door, and `sidecar_law_test.go` fails the build on one that does not.
  - A READING THAT LANDS LATE IS APPLIED, NOT DROPPED. A routed memory block that arrives before the request is assembled rides it; one that arrives before the first token CUTS the request and re-asks once (`errRecallCut`, steer.go — no backoff, no journal row, nothing on the person's screen because there was nothing there yet); one that arrives after the first token rides the NEXT step and the turn's journal row says `recall:late`. A drawing with independent parts in it cuts the step in flight (`errMarkCut`) through the same door a person's steer uses. `Agent.cutGeneration(cause)` is that door and is new; `errSteerCut` is unchanged.
  - `keepSteeredPartial` TAKES A FIFTH ARGUMENT, the sentence explaining a dropped half-arrived tool call. There are two doors into the boundary a cut opens now, and a record that told the model it had been steered when a sidecar had read the turn would be putting words in somebody's mouth (`cutDroppedCallNote`, loop.go).
  - THE TWO END-OF-TURN READERS RUN AGAINST EACH OTHER, not one after the other, AND THE JUDGE DECIDES WHERE IT USED TO ACT. `Agent.routeJudge` is split: `Agent.readRouteJudge` answers a `judgeRuling` and starts nothing, `Agent.applyRouteJudge` is the only thing with an effect in it, and the TURN calls it — after the re-open reader has said it will neither re-open nor move the turn. It used to launch the task from inside its own goroutine, which meant the effect landed whenever its two calls happened to return rather than at the moment the turn could still spend it: a fast screen and confirm put work on the rail over the top of a turn that was about to be re-opened or handed over. A ruling nobody applies releases the name it was holding (`judgeRace.end`). `judgeRace` carries a `sidecar[judgeRuling]` where it carried a `sidecar[struct{}]`.
  - `Agent.askRouteJudge` AND `Agent.confirmRouteWork` HAVE WINDOWS. They had none, inheriting the LOW tier's two minutes and the MASTERMIND tier's TEN, at the end of a turn with the person's answer already on their screen. They now carry `routeRaceWindow` (20s) and `routeRaceConfirmWindow` (30s) — the same windows their pre-turn twins have always had.
  - `lane.RoleRecall` PATIENCE IS 0.2, NOT 1: a 2-second ceiling and an 18-second give-up. And `internal/reflex`'s `Route` bounds itself at `lane.RoleRecall.GiveUp()` where it read `Ceiling()`. Those two were the same instant, which meant the hazard controller was told to act on a silent recall at exactly the moment the deadline killed it — so no recall in this build's history was ever moved off a slow machine. Two seconds is above the fastest measured reflex machine's median (DeepInfra 1.7s) and below the slow ones' (Io Net 4.3s, DekaLLM 5.5s).
  - `lane.RoleJudge` PATIENCE IS 1, NOT 6: a 10-second ceiling and a 90-second give-up. Sixty seconds was outside every window its callers set, so nothing was ever moved off a silent judge machine, and the same census has four mark readings dying at 30,001–30,002 ms having decided nothing. The quantity is recall's quantity read against a caller's window rather than a machine's median: LATE ENOUGH that a healthy machine is never abandoned mid-answer (above the measured first token, 8.4s at the ninetieth) and EARLY ENOUGH that a second machine can still answer inside the window the caller allows (that window less the same 8.4s). The tightest window that constrains it is the pre-turn route read's 20s, so the interval is (8.4s, 11.6s) and ten seconds is in it and is `lane.VisiblePatience` itself. The guardian's 10s is NOT one of those windows and the table says why: when it goes quiet the fall-through is to ASK THE PERSON, so a rescue there buys nothing.
  - THE SAFETY GATE DRAWS A PHASE WORD, OVER THE TOP OF THE BATCH'S OWN. `guardianAllows` blocked a tool call for up to ten seconds with nothing on the screen; it now posts `checking whether this is safe to run` for the whole window through `Agent.interruptPhase` (new, phasenews.go), which hands back the phase that was being held so the batch's `running <tool>` word comes BACK rather than being cleared — the phase is one slot, and this gate runs inside a batch that may have minutes left. It is THE ONE NAMED EXCEPTION to the law below — it decides whether a tool RUNS, so there is nothing to run beside it and nothing it could be applied to afterwards — and loop.go's header, guardian.go, `permissions.md` and `screen.md` all say so.
  - A SLOW LISTENER NO LONGER HOLDS THE ENGINE'S GOROUTINE. `postPhaseNews` (phasenews.go) and `postLaneNews` (lanenews.go) both said in their own doc comments that they never block on a slow reader, and both of them called the reader DOWN THE TELLER'S OWN STACK — so the last act of every model call, `phase.done()`, paid a whole Bubble Tea Update-and-View cycle before the engine goroutine got its call back, because `internal/tui3` asks for a frame through an unbuffered channel. On every call, not only a cancelled one. Both doors now leave the news on a `desk` (sidecar.go — the same file and the same law as `readBeside`, read from the other end: one goroutine per desk at a time, order kept, nothing coalesced and nothing dropped, because lane news is a ledger). `internal/session`'s own test helpers wait on the desk (`phaseLog.all`, and `hears` hands back a function where it handed back a slice); `internal/remote` and `internal/enginehost` already polled.
  - `Agent.Close` SETTLES THE WRITES IT OWES TWICE — once on the way in for what was owed before it, and once at the end for what the close ITSELF sets in motion: a node stopped, a follow-up dropped, a place referred on the way out each owe a write, and every one of those happens in the rounds between. The first call is above `a.mu.Lock()` and the second is past where the lock is released, which is the whole of `SettleWrites`' own contract. #876 landed `Agent.SettleWrites` — the one exit door for a deferred write behind a person's path (the meta.json stamp, the fix shelf's counters, a folder referred but not yet cut) — and named `Agent.Close` as where it belongs, but nothing called it there, so an owed write had an exit window of one write's length. It is called beside `Agent.settleDeliveries` and BEFORE the `a.mu.Lock()` that follows, because every write it waits on takes that lock.
  - A SESSION'S DEFERRED WRITES ARE SETTLED AFTER THE CLOSE AND NOT IN FRONT OF IT. `newTestAgent` registered the two cleanups the wrong way round, so the settle ran on what the session owed a moment ago while what the CLOSE itself sets in motion — a node stopped, a follow-up dropped, a place referred on the way out — landed on a directory the runner had already taken away (`TempDir RemoveAll cleanup: directory not empty`). `Agent.Close` settles on its own way in now, so the pre-close settle bought nothing anyway. `stampedMeta` goes through the same door before it reads; `metaOnDisk` is the plain reader for a test with no session behind it.
  - `internal/remote`'s `TestAnOlderEnginesNewsFrameLandsWithNoConversationOnIt` WAITS FOR THE DESK, the way every other test on that page already waits: the news is handed on by the desk's own goroutine now, so arriving is a moment later than posting. And `TestASubmissionStampsTheFolder` (place_test.go) goes through `Agent.SettleWrites` before it reads `meta.json` back, which is what that method's own doc asks of every test that reads one of those files — the last-active stamp is a deferred write (#876) and reading it without settling gets whatever the scheduler had got to, which on a loaded machine is the zero time.
  - #876's `TestConsultingTheFixStoreWritesNothingOnThePath` IS DETERMINISTIC. It consulted the fix shelf five times and then stat-ed the file, but `offpath.Write.Owe` starts its goroutine at once and that goroutine is as entitled to the processor as the test's — so the assertion asked whether the scheduler got there first, and on a loaded box it did (met on Spark at `db6ed4ed5`, red in both `test-laws` and `touched packages`). The deferred write is HELD while the read path runs now, so the file can only exist if the read path itself wrote it, which is the whole claim.
  - EVERY TURN WRITES A `pace` LINE. `journalPace` (sessionfile.go) carries `sendMs`, `firstWordMs`, `stepGapMs`, `steps` and which readings were in flight beside the work. Nothing recorded those before: the 2026-09-11 audit reconstructed them by subtracting request stamps out of `calls.jsonl`, which is how a four-second gate in front of every message went unnoticed for as long as it did. A replay ignores the line.
  - `internal/reflex`'s `TestRecallSharesTheInteractiveDeadlineAcrossRepair` IS RENAMED `TestRecallSharesTheRolesGiveUpAcrossRepair` and asserts `lane.RoleRecall.GiveUp()` where it asserted `lane.VisiblePatience`. The old name encoded the bug.

  THE LAW, stated in loop.go's header and guarded by two tests: **the only wait a
  person experiences is the main model generating**. Every reading this harness
  makes on its own behalf — which remembered lines a message needs, what is left of
  a long answer, whether a message was really work, a name, a caption — runs BESIDE
  the work and may only INTERRUPT it. A person's message reaches the wire within
  50 ms, and so does a tool result.

  Quality is kept by APPLYING every decision rather than by awaiting it: in time,
  and it is spent on this step; late, and it is spent on the next one or written
  down as late. Nothing is dropped, because a dropped reading is a reading whose
  ledger never learns.

  </details>

- **a machine is asked only when the answer is expected inside the wait its work will sit through** — [#873](https://github.com/Agent-Field/codeaf/pull/873) · `engine` `chat` `docs`

  <details><summary>8 things that are no longer true</summary>

  - A probe could ride a role somebody is waiting on. `sheetDoubtsLast` promoted the best doubted machine to the front of one request in ten with no regard for who was waiting on that request — one request spent settling a doubt every later request profits from, which is a good bet on an errand and a bad one in front of a keypress, where the whole of the call is dead time. The promotion is now off for every role the table declares `Interactive`, which is a property of the role and not a list of them; the demotion is unchanged, because ranking a doubted machine last costs nobody anything. `TestNoProbeRidesARoleSomebodyIsWaitingOn` walks the whole role table in both directions, so a role added to it tomorrow is covered without anybody remembering the test exists.
  - The chooser ranked by a median and refused by nothing. A machine was sampled, scored and ordered, and the only absolute opinion anywhere was the service floor's `FloorTTFT`/`FloorRate` — figures about machines nobody would keep, not about what THIS work will wait for. There is now one reading, `rolePatience.expected`: how long a request is expected to take to a usable answer on one machine — the first-token and rate posteriors at the quantile this role is exposed to, widened by the machine's own MEASURED one-answer dispersion (`Belief.Spread`), divided by `Belief.Serving`. The order is that number sorted and the refusal is that number against the role's own declared ceiling (`beyondThePatience`). There is no ratio, no threshold anybody chose, and no rule anywhere naming a role or a machine.
  - `provider.order` was where a refusal went. It is a RANKING the router may ignore once `allow_fallbacks` is true (#850 said so and did not finish acting on it): on 2026-09-11 09:33:10 a reflex call asked for DeepInfra and DekaLLM answered. A machine the role refuses now reaches `provider.ignore`, which is the only half a router honours, and `refusedInto` is not gated on λ the way `ignoredOf` is — that door refuses a machine for being slower than another, which is an objective a request with nobody waiting does not have, while this one carries a refusal the role made out of its own patience.
  - A warm prompt prefix outranked everything. The cache affinity pin latches onto whichever machine ANSWERED (`affinity.go`) and is prepended to the next request's order, so ONE router deviation made that machine the head of every order for the rest of the session — which is the whole of six of seventeen reflex calls going to a machine nothing had ever measured, at 5.5s against 1.8s. A saving on prefill may not buy a wait the role has already refused: `applyLaneChoice` drops the affinity head when `choice.Ignore` names it.
  - Whether a person READS an answer was read from the two-valued routing intent. A recall is `Interactive` — somebody is sitting in front of it — and `Visible: false`, because nobody reads a word of what it writes: it goes into a prompt. Read through the intent, all of its tokens were counted as text somebody is reading, and `PerceivedSeconds` charges read text only for the part arriving slower than `ReadRate`. Four hundred tokens at fifteen a second were therefore priced at four seconds when the truth was twenty-six, and no chooser reading that number could refuse a slow writer for a call nobody reads. `workloadFor` reads the role's own `Visible` column where the call named a role, and falls back to the intent where it did not.
  - A change point reset the chain's own component and left the flat belief the chooser reads exactly where it was. The CUSUM in `chains.note` already watched both the wait and the rate chains and already alarmed; what it reset was the hierarchy's pair level, while `Belief.TTFT` and `Belief.Rate` — the two posteriors `Chooser.Choose` actually samples — went on damping every new reading with fifty old ones about a machine that no longer existed. Measured on 2026-09-11: one machine's generation rate fell about ninefold at 09:33 and it was still being chosen five steps later over thirty-three minutes, one of those answers nine minutes long. A change point is a statement that the old evidence is about a different machine, so the flat belief now adopts the observation outright (`stepTo`) exactly as `Posterior.Update` already does for a belief that knows nothing. No second detector was added.
  - `Belief` carried no measurement of how far ONE answer sits from its median, and `Posterior.P` cannot stand in for one — it is the variance of the ESTIMATE and shrinks toward nothing after a few dozen observations, which is `SpreadFloor`'s own stated law. A machine answering in a second half the time and in a minute the other half therefore had a median nothing was unsure about and a tail that was the whole of what a person paid. `Belief.Spread` is that dispersion, measured with the three floats and the pooled-and-floored arithmetic a thinking duration already keeps (`chains.widen`, `chains.draw`), folded on the same lock and in the same call as the median beside it. It may only ever be WIDER than the sheet's published figure (`ledger.seenSpread`): a handful of similar answers is not evidence that a machine's tail is rarer than its publisher says. It is FORGOTTEN with the median when a change point fires — `chains.widen` is Welford with no forgetting of any kind and it is persisted, so the distance between two regimes would otherwise land in its sum of squares permanently and a machine that had one bad hour would be widened by exp(z90·σ) for the life of the file, refusable for ever on a tail it no longer has. That is the absorbing gate this package ended everywhere else. `Ledger.Draw`, which is the hazard's question and not the chooser's, is unchanged, and the rate chain keeps no dispersion account at all: a rate that moves within a regime is what its posterior covers and a rate that moves between regimes is the change point's job.
  - `lane.Request` said nothing about who a call was for. It carries `Role` now — whole, rather than flattened into the two or three numbers a chooser happens to want today, because a field holding one column would be a second table to keep in step with the first. `provider.callKnobs` resolves it once at the top of the call beside `intent`, for `intent`'s reason: it is a fact about the CALLER and the encoder has no context to ask. An empty role has NO DEADLINE and therefore refuses nothing: `RoleUnknown`'s row is a good default for how a call is treated and a bad answer to what it is unwilling to wait for, because nobody said — reading its thirty seconds as a declared deadline would strike machines off the wire's table on behalf of every call site in the tree that has not yet been taught to name itself. `patienceFor` leaves the ceiling at zero for an unnamed role, which is the same reading `internal/provider`'s `workloadFor` keeps at the other end of the seam, so the two packages cannot come to mean different things by "unknown".

  Replicated from the call log rather than described. `internal/lane/rolepatience_test.go`
  replays the 09:33 rate collapse (forty-five answers at sixty tokens a second, then three
  at six) and asserts the belief follows within three, and stages the 10:02 task step as a
  machine with a healthy first token, a rate above `FloorRate`, and an answer no role that
  somebody watches will wait for. `internal/provider/rolepatience_test.go` asserts on the
  request as it arrived at a `lanestub` router: the refused machine on `ignore` and not
  merely off the order, the cache affinity pin losing to the refusal, and no probe in front
  of two hundred consecutive calls somebody is waiting on.

  Two laws ride the `laws` gate. `TestTheChoiceNamesNoRoleAndNoMachine` walks `choose.go`
  and `frontier.go` with `go/ast` and fails on any comparison against a `Role` constant or
  between a lane and a string literal — proved by planting both and watching it name the
  lines. `TestNoProbeRidesARoleSomebodyIsWaitingOn` walks the whole role table in both
  directions. Beside them `TestTwoRolesWithTheSameColumnsGetTheSameChoice` asserts the
  behavioural half: two roles the table describes identically are answered identically over
  one pool, which found a real difference on its first run (`Horizon` is a fourth declared
  column the chooser reads, and it belongs in the comparison).

  Still owed and written up in the lane report rather than worked around here: the hazard's
  mid-stream `rate collapsed` test (`hazard.keepingUp`) compares the live gap to the SERVED
  machine's own belief, so a machine that is normally slow is never surprising to itself and
  the first slow stream is not moved off. The seam is `control.Plan` carrying what the pool's
  best admissible machine is believed to give, which crosses `lane.PlanFor` and the control
  contract #858/#864 just landed.

  </details>

- **the frame reads a memo and never the disk, and a go/ast law keeps it that way** — [#875](https://github.com/Agent-Field/codeaf/pull/875) · `chat` `build` `docs`

  <details><summary>12 things that are no longer true</summary>

  - The frame stat'd every visible picture on every paint. `(*app).picture` took an `os.Stat` before the cache lookup because the file's modification time and size WERE the preview cache's key — twelve open pictures at 30 Hz was 360 syscalls a second, taken from inside `View`. The key is the same key; what is in it is now a fact the LOOP learned (`internal/tui3/learned.go`), read at `open`, on the pulse's ten-second beat, and at each arrival — the picture call ending, the file being attached, the mirror's copy landing, the press that expands a collapsed picture.
  - `/workspace <path>` probed git ON the loop. It called `a.gitProbe(resolved)` straight, which is `git rev-parse` and `git status` under one shared 400 ms ceiling, so the surface froze for up to four tenths of a second on the keystroke that set the workspace. It takes `probeGit` now — the off-loop road every other reading of the repository already took — and the branch arrives as a `gitMsg`, so the legend draws nothing for a moment rather than everything freezing.
  - `CachedModels`/`CachedModelsFor` were read straight from the render path. Every frame that had to name a model with no catalog behind it — the first-run screen, every window opened with no key — re-read `~/.aforge/v3/models.json` in full. The frame reads `app.cachedModelsFor`, a memo filled at `open` (`app.learnModelLists`), refreshed on the beat, and dropped by name when ctrl+r's fetch or a service connection rewrites that file.
  - There was no check on ARCHITECTURE.md's fourth law. `internal/tui3/framedisk_law_test.go` now walks this package with go/ast from `(*app).View` — through calls on the surface, package functions, and func-typed FIELDS by what is assigned to them — and fails on `os.Stat`, `os.ReadFile`, `os.Open`, `exec.Command`, `filepath.Glob` or the network. A sibling asks the update loop the narrower question (no process, no wire, on the loop) and walks every closure except the ones handed off as commands. The allowlist is one entry: the picture decode.
  - A job's page took its log's first reading inside the frame (`jobPageSeed`, one `os.Open` per page open, from the layout). It is deleted: `showJobPage` has one caller, `openJobPage`, and that caller has always followed it with `jobPageArm`, which opens the same file off the loop and starts the beat that keeps it moving.
  - A bare notice board went through the ledger LOADER to conclude it had no ledger. `noticeEvent`'s fallback mints one (`bareNoticeBoard`) instead, so no file read is on the graph of what a frame can reach.
  - The model shelf read a service's cache file from inside a draw. `v3ModelShelf.modelsForService` (cmd/aforge) fell through to `tui3.CachedModelsFor` whenever its compartment was empty — an `os.ReadFile` and a JSON parse of the whole list, taken through `Options.ModelsForService` from tui3's own `setupModelRows`, on every paint of the first-run screen for a profile with two model services. An empty compartment is an empty answer now; `setSources` fills the compartments off the frame and tui3's memo is the one disk rung on its side.
  - The update loop started a process on a keystroke. `processOpener` is a package-level var holding `startOpener`, which ran `exec.Command(...).Start()` synchronously from ctrl+o, `o open folder`, /connect, the first-run sign-in and /files. The name is still resolved on the loop — `exec.Command` records a PATH miss without forking, and that miss is the answer those doors say `no way to open` from — but the fork and the wait are on a guard goroutine.
  - The law could not see a func VAR or a door-installed field. Seams came only from `a.field = fn`, so `var processOpener = startOpener` and `modelsForService: opts.ModelsForService` were both invisible, and `TestTheUpdateLoopStartsNoProcessOfItsOwn` was green while the loop started a process. The walk now collects field assignments, `var` declarations, composite-literal keys and function literals written into any of them — and `TestTheLawSeesEveryShapeOfIndirectionItClaims` plants each shape in a source of its own and fails if the walk goes blind to one.
  - `TestTheUpdateLoopStartsNoProcessOfItsOwn` asked whether `exec.Command` was called. Building a command resolves a name on PATH and starts nothing, which a door that must answer on the frame that needs it may do; what the loop may not do is START one. The rule is now `Start`/`Run`/`Output`/`CombinedOutput`/`Wait` on a name the same body bound to `exec.Command`, and the allowlist is empty again.
  - `modelsFetched` dropped the model memo BEFORE it checked whether the fetch had failed, so a failed refresh — which writes nothing — threw away a good reading and left the next frame on the built-ins. The drop is after the check.
  - A file rewritten behind a running window is noticed on the pulse's beat rather than by the next frame. Nothing on a machine tells a terminal that a png was overwritten or that another process rewrote the model cache; the frame no longer asks, so the ten-second beat and the arrival that changed the bytes are the two ways it is learned. A test that rewrites one of those files mid-run has to say so (`a.refreshLearning()`), which is what the beat stands in for.

  Three readings, one shape: *a fact read off the disk under a name, kept until
  something says the bytes moved*. So there is ONE mechanism for it — `learned[T]`
  — with three doors and a rule about which loop may open each: `of` is the
  frame's and reads nothing, `learn` is the loop's and is called by `open`, by a
  tick and by an arrival, `refresh` is the beat. `catchUp` reads whatever the last
  frame asked about, once, on the loop, which makes the arrival hooks a matter of
  latency rather than of correctness.

  Measured on `BenchmarkFramePictures` (new): a dozen expanded pictures on a
  100×40 frame, M3 Max, 3000× × 5 — **328 µs** a frame against a **360 µs** median
  and a **528 µs** syscall-stall tail before.

  </details>

- **nothing hidden happens on a turn — one file memo, one off-path reading, one deferred write** — [#876](https://github.com/Agent-Field/codeaf/pull/876) · `chat` `engine` `docs`

  <details><summary>10 things that are no longer true</summary>

  - `read` on a picture, a recording or a video made an untagged, unannounced model call that could run for the ten-minute general completion bound. Every model call a HAND makes now goes through one door (`internal/session/toolask.go`): tagged `tool:<name>` in the call log, carrying the node inside a task, drawing a phase the person reads (`looking at error.png`, `listening to memo.m4a`, `watching run.mp4`), and bounded by `lane.RoleTool.GiveUp()`. A structural law fails the build on any `tools_*.go` that calls `completeWithModel` itself.
  - `view_image` carried its own ten-minute window, `viewLookWindow = providerTimeout`. That var is DELETED. The bound is the role's — `lane.RoleTool` is a new row whose patience says a person is watching the tool row it holds open, so the give-up is ninety seconds and something is done about silence at ten. Its refusal still names the model and the file; the duration in it is now the role's.
  - A `max_tokens` on a hand's question looks like the fix for a 10 s wait and is NOT sent, deliberately, with a law that fails the build on the next attempt (`TestAHandSendsNoOutputCeiling`). The only principled ceiling is the belt's own tool-result cap, which is ~12,500 tokens against measured answers of 588–1,256 and therefore never binds — and internal/lane's gate rules a machine OUT when its published `MaxOut` is below the request's `max_tokens` (`frontier.go`'s `capable`), so sending it would strike vision machines off the serving set of the very tool it was meant to speed up. What bounds the wait is the role; what makes it visible is the phase.
  - `git status --untracked-files=all` ran INLINE in every batch of ordinary chat that contained a shell command — ten to thirty milliseconds on a small repository, seconds on a large one, between the tools finishing and the next request being assembled. It is now taken with `offpath.Take` and settled at `lane.Hysteresis`, the quantity this build already calls the smallest difference in waiting anybody notices. A repository git can read inside that behaves exactly as before; one it cannot has the reading folded by the next batch instead of blocking the turn.
  - `compactToolHistory` rebuilt the reduced form of the FROZEN prefix from scratch on every request of every tool round — a SHA-256 over the whole of every old tool result to find its pointer, a fresh copy of its text, a fresh view — work proportional to everything the conversation had ever read, paid again on each request. It is memoised per message on the agent (`Agent.toolCompact`), guarded per index by the result's call id and its byte weight, so a message the stubbing pass rewrote is recomputed and nothing else is. Measured: 1.34 ms → 13 µs at 100 rounds, 11.7 ms → 156 µs at 1600. `compactToolHistory` is now a method; loop.go's call site gained `a.`.
  - The profile's `config.json` was read and parsed on EVERY call — `APIKeyConfigured` on every Enter, `FirstPrompt` on every turn, eight readers in `internal/config`. `readProfileConfig` now goes through `filememo.Stamped(SettingsGeneration, …)`: one stat per call, a parse only when the file's size or timestamp moved or this process persisted a write. The comment saying this package deliberately holds no cache is rewritten rather than left standing. `writeProfileValues` copies before adding its row, because the map a reader holds is the memo's.
  - `renderSystemAt` re-read AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md whenever the prompt's clock went stale — the came-back-to-the-terminal turn, and once per attached folder. `readInstructionFileWithin` now goes through the same `filememo` type, holding the bytes so a lean bound and a full bound share one read.
  - `fixShelf.consult` — the READ path, asked after every failed tool call — persisted its two counters, four whole-file read-modify-write cycles per fail→fix→succeed iteration under a process-global lock. It writes nothing now. The counters are owed to `offpath.Write` and land behind the path or at `fixStore.settle()`.
  - `stampUserLocked` did a whole `LoadMeta` + `SaveMeta` — read, MkdirAll, CreateTemp, write, rename — WITH THE AGENT LOCK HELD, in the moment between a person pressing Enter and their turn starting. The snapshot is still taken on the path; the disk is `offpath.Write`'s, coalesced so two messages a second apart owe one write, and `Agent.SettleWrites()` is the exit door for it and for every other deferred write in this change.
  - A conversation's working copy of a referred folder — a `git worktree add`, or a whole recursive copy — was cut INSIDE the first tool call that wrote a file, silently. It is now started when the folder is referred (`Agent.ReferPlace` → `Agent.startStandingTree`), so it runs while the person reads their own screen, and it says `preparing · a working copy of <folder>` for as long as it lasts wherever it runs. A cut that cannot be made is still not a refusal: the write goes to the real folder. Both roads to a copy now ask one named predicate, `keptAside` — the folder you are standing in is never copied, and neither is one you said to work in directly — rather than the head start having a weaker answer of its own than the write path. And because a mode can only be said AFTER the place is referred, saying "in place" now settles the head start and gives an untouched copy back, worktree and branch (`git branch -d`, so git's own refusal protects a branch holding a commit); a copy something has been written into is never taken back.

  Three mechanisms, not eleven patches. `internal/filememo` is "a file read at most
  once per change" (config.json, AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md); `internal/offpath` is the
  two shapes of work that must not happen on a person's path — `Take`/`Reading`
  for a fact gathered beside the work and `Deferred`/`Write` for a write a read
  path owes; `internal/session/toolask.go` is the one door a hand asks a model
  through. Each carries its law in its doc comment and a test that fails the build
  on the next copy of it.

  Not memoised, deliberately: `fixStore.saveLocked` and `Agent.updateMeta` both
  re-read their file inside a read-modify-write so that another window's
  simultaneous change survives the merge. A memo there would be a memo in front of
  a WRITE, which is a different thing with a different law.

  </details>

- **A quick task comes through one door, its checkpoint rebuilds it, and it holds the files it wrote** — [#879](https://github.com/Agent-Field/codeaf/pull/879) · `chat` `engine` `docs`

  <details><summary>11 things that are no longer true</summary>

  - #869 expected that once the record carried a quick node's list, a queued quick node could resume as a quick node instead of settling. The list is carried now, and a queued quick node still settles: the turn that asked for it is over, and it would run in the new session's folder rather than its caller's.
  - `taskRecord` carried a quick node's kind and not its body, so a restored quick node had `spec.quick == nil` and its ticks were lost. The record now carries `quick: {line, items, done, files}`, a tick checkpoints, and `restoreNode` rebuilds the body.
  - A quick node was settled on restart only if it was running, and it was counted as `interrupted (no branch kept)`. A quick node that was running or still queued now settles as `failed`, its report lists which items were ticked and which were not, and the recovery line counts it as `N quick tasks did not finish`.
  - `continue task N` re-queued a quick task, and a restored one then ran as an ordinary worker in a worktree. It is now refused with `task N is quick, not a run that can be continued`.
  - The ceiling's handover admitted its quick node through `launchRouteTask(…, quick)`, with an invented acceptance, a worktree mode, a naming call and depth 0. Every quick node now comes through `Agent.admitQuick(quickAsk)`, and `launchRouteTask` no longer takes a quick parameter.
  - `fileOwner` held written files only for nodes with a branch, so a running quick task held nothing and the chat could overwrite a file it had half-written. Every running node that does not hold its whole tree (`TaskNode.holdsTreeLocked`) now owns the paths it has written, and a write to one of them is refused with the holder named (`<file> is held by task N (<title>), so nothing was written.`).
  - The chat manual said a file a quick task *named* at the start is held against the chat. It is not. Only files it has written are held; a named file only makes a second quick task that names the same file wait.
  - `PresenceTask` had no kind or parent, and `<elsewhere>` listed another window's quick parts as separate rows. It now carries `kind` and `parent`, plus `done`/`total` taken from a quick task's items, and the block folds the parts onto their head row (`3 quick parts running`).
  - The ceiling's handover started a naming request before it knew which road the turn was taking, so every write-free carry-on paid a model for a name a quick node can never use. The request is now made below that branch, and a quick carry-on asks for no name at all.
